explanation: Steam usually makes up the largest share of volcanic gas. Carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide typically come next, and hydrogen sulfide gives some vents their rotten-egg smell.

claims.text: Water vapour is typically the most abundant gas released by volcanoes.
Carbon dioxide, sulfur dioxide and hydrogen sulfide are each usually less abundant in volcanic gas than water vapour.
After water vapour, carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide are typically the most abundant volcanic gases.
Hydrogen sulfide, released at some volcanic vents, smells of rotten eggs.

writerNotes: Self-check (CONTENT_GUIDE 9.3). lint: content:check run on the batch. claims: all listed; c1 is the key of a counterintuitive item and, like c2 and c3, a superlative (high). datasets: none covers volcanic gas. One writer search for c1 to c3: query 'most abundant volcanic gas water vapor USGS'; results included usgs.gov (volcanic gas), pubs.usgs.gov (Open-File Reports 97-262 and 95-85) and a USGS Volcano Hazards Program page archived at webarchive.library.unt.edu; the summary said USGS sources consistently identify water vapour as the most abundant volcanic gas, followed by carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, and that concentrations vary considerably from one volcano to the next. rivalTest: players picture choking smoke and pick carbon dioxide or sulfur dioxide; that is the trap the explanation defuses. Against the key: some vents and some volcanoes can be carbon-dioxide rich, which is why the stem says 'usually' and the claims say 'typically'. volatility: evergreen. regional: no local knowledge. style: Oxford spelling (vapour) with IUPAC sulfur, explanation 27 words. myths: screened; no hit. mystery and encore: not applicable. doubts: the word 'usually' carries the item; I am comfortable with it given the USGS wording. evidence.summaryExcerpt: USGS sources consistently identify water vapor as the most abundant volcanic gas, followed by carbon dioxide and then sulfur dioxide. A 1995 USGS report says water vapor is typically the most abundant volcanic gas, followed by carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide.

claimResults.note: Every result is a USGS page or an archived copy of one, so the call counts at Tier A. Rival test: at some hot, high-flux vents (for example Kilauea's summit) CO2 can match or top water in the plume, and the plume's water is dwarfed by atmospheric water, so 'carbon dioxide' has a defensible reading. The stem says 'usually' and the claim says 'typically', matching the USGS wording, so it holds.
